Moores Lab AI’s Benchmark Push: Measuring Whether AI Can Actually Verify Chipsby Daniel Nenni on 11-24-2026 at 10:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: EDA, Moores Lab (AI)

Key takeaways ▼
AI tools can generate hardware code quickly. The harder question is whether they can establish that a design behaves correctly. Moores Lab AI’s benchmark initiative addresses that distinction, putting attention on verification outcomes rather than the volume or apparent sophistication of generated code. For semiconductor teams evaluating automation, that shift could make performance claims more useful.
In its October announcement, Moores Lab AI described a planned public benchmark where users could run their verification environments against designs containing known, hidden bugs. The proposed test asks a practical question: which defects does the environment actually detect? That is a different standard from merely producing a testbench that compiles or runs without errors.
I spoke to Shelly Henry, he is one of the more personable CEOs you will ever meet, also one of the most intelligent and experienced:
“After decades in design verification engineering, I know verification is about much more than just writing a compiling code. It’s about finding RTL bugs. It’s about protocol correctness. It’s about finding the corner cases, writing the correct assertions and coverage. The details are what determine whether you can trust the results. That’s why we are building the Moores Lab Verification Benchmark, a way to measure verification work against real design verification challenges.”

The announcement followed the company’s evaluation on NVIDIA’s Comprehensive Verilog Design Problems benchmark, or CVDP. Moores Lab AI reported a 93% overall pass rate on a selected verification subset and 100% for stimulus generation. Its evaluation covered stimulus, checker and assertion generation, with each problem attempted once inside a container using a commercial simulator and hidden grading tests.
The qualification matters. Although the original subset contained 62 problems, Moores Lab AI excluded six, stating that their hidden graders contradicted the supplied requirements. All compared configurations were scored on the remaining 56. Accordingly, the reported 93% should be described as performance on that adjusted subset, rather than a score across the entire CVDP benchmark or proof of complete verification capability.
NVIDIA’s public infrastructure provides useful context. CVDP supports both direct language-model evaluation and agentic workflows, allowing systems to interact with execution environments. Its tooling supports repeated sampling, records evaluation outputs and accommodates commercial verification tools where required. These details matter because a model’s answer and an agent’s completed engineering task are different things, requiring appropriately controlled comparisons.
My interpretation is that the surrounding workflow deserves as much scrutiny as the underlying model. An effective agent must interpret requirements, create useful artifacts, execute tools, understand failures and revise its work. Buyers should therefore compare complete configurations, including simulator access, available context, iteration limits and computational budgets. Otherwise, an apparent model advantage may partly reflect differences in the evaluation environment.
Why does this matter? Verification code can look convincing while checking the wrong behavior. A test can stimulate a design without detecting an incorrect response. A checker can encode an assumption that the specification never established. Moores Lab AI’s own specification discussion warns that invented requirements can propagate into scoreboards and tests, producing misleading passes rather than trustworthy evidence.
Testing against hidden defects offers one way to challenge that false confidence. In principle, it rewards environments that expose incorrect behavior, rather than environments that simply execute successfully. However, the strength of that evidence depends on the defects themselves: how representative they are, whether they cover meaningful failure modes and whether correct designs are also accepted without excessive false alarms.
For engineering managers, benchmark results should guide a pilot rather than replace one. A useful evaluation would measure detected bugs, missed bugs, false positives, engineer intervention, runtime and cost on representative internal designs. Teams should also examine whether generated verification artifacts remain understandable and maintainable after the initial demonstration. These are purchasing criteria, not capabilities established by a headline pass rate.
Bottom line: The broader significance is a move toward measurable engineering accountability. NVIDIA’s repository notes that Si2 is adopting CVDP into its LLM Benchmarking Coalition, extending categories and refining metrics. Shared evaluation infrastructure can help customers compare systems more consistently. Moores Lab AI’s initiative contributes to that conversation, but independent reproduction and transparent methodology will determine its lasting value. The commercial prize is faster verification with defensible confidence: evidence that automation finds consequential mistakes before they become silicon, while reducing the engineering effort needed to reach that conclusion.
